evt-pj-emperor-keitai: A statue of Emperor Keitai, the sovereign who founded a new line within the Yamato dynasty.
evt-pj-soga-rise: A shrine tied to the Soga, the clan that rose to dominate the Yamato court.
evt-pj-baekje-artisans: Yuzuki no Kimi, the legendary immigrant leader said to have brought continental artisans to Yamato.
evt-pj-buddhism-arrives: The Asuka-dera Great Buddha, Japan's oldest surviving Buddhist statue, from soon after the faith arrived.
evt-pj-obsidian-trade: Chunks of obsidian from Hoshikuso Pass, the glassy volcanic stone the Jomon quarried and traded across hundreds of miles.
evt-pj-jomon-jade: A string of comma-shaped magatama beads, the curved jade ornaments the Jomon ground and polished by hand.
evt-pj-jomon-dogs: The skull of a Jomon dog, an animal valued enough to be buried with care rather than eaten.
evt-pj-yayoi-warfare: A bronze Yayoi spearhead, a weapon-form from the era when moated villages began bristling with defenses.
evt-pj-baekje-alliance: The Seven-Branched Sword, the inscribed Baekje gift that seals the alliance between the Korean kingdom and Yamato.
evt-pj-yamato-hegemony: The gold-inlaid inscription on an iron sword naming the great king Wakatakeru, hard proof of Yamato's reach.
evt-kush-independence: The Kushite heartland around Napata and Meroë, with the empire at its 25th-Dynasty peak stretching down the Nile to the Mediterranean.
evt-kush-napata-state: Gebel Barkal, the flat-topped sacred mountain beside Napata that the Kushites held to be the true home of the god Amun.
evt-el-kurru-pyramids: The main pyramid mound at El-Kurru, the early royal cemetery where Kush's first kings were buried with a long descending stairway to the tomb chamber.
evt-gold-trade: A gold flower-shaped diadem from a royal pyramid at Nuri — the kind of fine goldwork that made Kushite gold famous across the ancient world.
evt-alara: The cartouche of Alara, the early Kushite founder-king, copied from a temple inscription by the 19th-century expedition of Karl Richard Lepsius.
evt-kashta: A bronze situla (ritual vessel) bearing the cartouches of King Kashta and his daughter Amenirdis — proof of Kush's reach into Egyptian Thebes.
evt-amenirdis: A relief of Amenirdis I, Kashta's daughter, installed at Thebes as God's Wife of Amun — the office that gave Kush a grip on Upper Egypt's holiest priesthood.
evt-piye-reign: The lunette of Piye's great stela, showing the king receiving the submission of defeated Egyptian rulers — the founding document of his reign.
evt-piye-conquest: A scene from Piye's victory stela: the conquered northern princes bow before the Kushite king, who is led a captured stallion as tribute.
evt-kush-piye-stela-detail: The granite Victory Stela of Piye, its dense hieroglyphic columns recording the campaign that put a Kushite king on Egypt's throne.
evt-piye-victory-stela: A line-drawing reconstruction of all four faces of Piye's Victory Stela — one of the longest royal narratives surviving from ancient Africa.
evt-shabaka: A granite head of Pharaoh Shabaka, the Kushite king who first ruled a unified Egypt from the Delta to Nubia.
evt-fall-of-memphis: An Assyrian palace relief from Nineveh showing the army storming an Egyptian city — the kind of assault that drove Kush out of Memphis.
evt-shabaka-stone: The Shabaka Stone, on which the Kushite king had an ancient Memphite creation text recopied — its center later hollowed out for use as a millstone.
evt-shebitku: A sculpted head of Shebitku, the Kushite pharaoh who took an aggressive stance against the rising power of Assyria.
evt-taharqa-reign: A statue of Taharqa, the greatest of the Kushite pharaohs, whose reign marked the high-water mark of the 25th Dynasty.
evt-taharqa-karnak: The lone surviving column of Taharqa's great kiosk at Karnak — all that remains of the Kushite king's monumental building at Egypt's chief temple.
evt-nuri-pyramids: The royal pyramids of Nuri, the burial ground founded by Taharqa where generations of Napatan kings were entombed.
evt-gebel-barkal-temples: The ruins of the great Amun temple (B500) at the foot of Gebel Barkal, the cult center the Kushite kings expanded into a vast complex.
evt-assyrian-invasion: The Neo-Assyrian Empire at its height, its armies pushing south to wrench Egypt away from Kushite control.
evt-tantamani: A statue of Tantamani, the last Kushite pharaoh of Egypt, who briefly retook the south before Assyria struck back.
evt-sack-thebes-663: Statues of Tantamani, whose reconquest provoked the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC — a catastrophe that ended Kushite rule in Egypt.
evt-amun-worship: A ram statue of Amun — the ram-headed god whose Napata cult sat at the very heart of Kushite kingship.
evt-psamtik-invasion: A statue of the Egyptian pharaoh Psamtik II, whose army raided deep into Nubia and sacked Napata around 593 BC.
evt-aspelta: A reconstructed statue of King Aspelta, who ruled Kush from Napata in the era after Egypt's raid and left detailed succession inscriptions.
evt-meroe-capital: The pyramid skyline of Meroë, the southern city that became Kush's capital and royal cemetery after Napata's decline.
evt-iron-smelting: The excavated royal city of Meroë, where vast mounds of slag testify to an iron industry that powered the kingdom for centuries.
evt-arkamani-i: A temple relief of King Arkamani (Ergamenes) at Dakka — the Greek-influenced ruler said to have broken the priests' old hold over the crown.
evt-meroitic-temples-amun: Ram statues lining a Meroitic temple approach, part of the Amun cult complexes the kings built across the Island of Meroë.
evt-meroe-pyramids: An aerial view of the Meroë necropolis, where steep-sided royal pyramids cluster by the dozen on the desert ridge.
evt-kush-meroitic-script-detail: The Meroitic alphabet, with its hieroglyphic and cursive signs and their tentative transcriptions — a script we can read aloud but still cannot fully understand.
evt-meroitic-script: A stone block from Meroë carved with cursive Meroitic — the first writing system developed for an indigenous African language.
evt-kush-apedemak: The Lion Temple at Naqa, dedicated to Apedemak, the lion-headed war god who was Kush's own — with no counterpart in the Egyptian pantheon.
evt-apedemak-cult: A relief of Apedemak rising as a serpent from a lotus at Naqa — an image of the lion god whose cult spread across Meroitic Kush.
evt-lion-temple-musawwarat: The Apedemak (Lion) Temple at Musawwarat es-Sufra, its sandstone walls carved with the war god and the kings who served him.
evt-kush-elephant-corps: A bronze figure of a mahout riding a war elephant — a reminder that Meroë trained the African elephants prized by ancient armies.
evt-kush-kandake-system: A carved bark-stand from Wad Ban Naga naming a ruling pair — evidence of the kandake tradition in which Kushite queens held real power.
evt-kandake-tradition: The pyramid of a Meroitic kandake at Meroë — these ruling queens were buried with the same royal honors as kings.
evt-meroitic-pottery: A painted Meroitic jar with a flowing vine pattern — the wheel-thrown fine ware that ranks among Kush's finest crafts.
evt-amanirenas: A temple relief of a Kushite queen enthroned with a lion at her feet — the warrior-ruler tradition embodied by Amanirenas.
evt-roman-war: The Hamadab Stela, inscribed in Meroitic, which commemorates the Kushite war against Rome under Queen Amanirenas.
evt-kush-bronze-head-augustus: The bronze head of Emperor Augustus, hacked from a Roman statue and carried home by the Kushites to be buried under a temple threshold at Meroë.
evt-augustus-bronze-head: The Meroë Head — the bronze portrait of Augustus that Kushite raiders took as a trophy and buried beneath a victory shrine so worshippers would tread on the emperor.
evt-treaty-of-samos: A Lepsius drawing of a crowned Kushite queen — the kind of ruler who negotiated the favorable peace with Rome settled at Samos in 21/20 BC.
evt-natakamani: A royal statue in the Sudan National Museum from the era of Natakamani and Amanitore, the co-rulers who presided over Meroë's golden age.
evt-amanitore: A carved bark-stand from Wad Ban Naga bearing the names of Queen Amanitore and her co-ruler Natakamani.
evt-lion-temple-naqa: The Lion Temple at Naqa, built by Natakamani and Amanitore for the war god Apedemak and decorated with their portraits.
evt-kush-amanishakheto: A relief of Queen Amanishakheto, a powerful Meroitic kandake whose pyramid at Meroë yielded a celebrated hoard of gold jewelry.
evt-kush-aksumite-end: Gold coins of an early Aksumite king — the rising Red Sea power that would seize the trade routes and help bring Kush to its end.
evt-aksumite-conquest: Gold coinage of King Ezana of Aksum, whose mid-4th-century campaign overran Meroë and closed the long history of Kush.
evt-royal-baths-meroe: The brick-built Royal Bath at Meroë, a sunken water basin ringed by columns that shows the Meroitic taste for monumental waterworks.
evt-ede-sahara-desiccation: A satellite view of the Sahara today — the green grassland that drew Egypt's earliest people had dried into this sea of sand by the time the kingdom rose.
evt-ede-nabta-playa: The Nabta Playa stone circle, reassembled near Aswan — a ring of small standing stones some call the world's oldest astronomical alignment.
evt-ede-cattle-culture: A black-topped red jar of the kind made by Egypt's cattle-herding predynastic communities, its dark rim a signature of early Nile pottery.
evt-ede-nile-farming: Flinders Petrie's catalogue of decorated predynastic pottery — the painted jars left behind by Egypt's first settled farming villages along the Nile.
evt-ede-fayum-agriculture: Flint arrowheads from the Fayum, where some of Egypt's earliest farmers planted grain beside a great lake.
evt-ede-merimde-settlement: A small clay head from Merimde Beni-Salame — one of the earliest human faces ever modelled in Egypt, from a village on the Delta's edge.
evt-ede-badarian-culture: A carved ivory female figurine of the kind buried with the Badarians, among the earliest Egyptian representations of the human form.
evt-ede-badarian-pottery: A Badarian bowl with the distinctive rippled, burnished surface — the hallmark of Egypt's finest early pottery, made before the wheel.
evt-ede-predynastic-burial: A predynastic grave with its body curled on its side amid pottery and beads — the goods packed in for a life beyond death.
evt-ede-maadi-culture: Dark basalt jars from Maadi in Lower Egypt, carved in the shapes of everyday pottery — the trading culture of the northern Delta.
evt-ede-naqada-i: Ivory figurines of the Naqada I (Amratian) culture of Upper Egypt, carved as the south's first towns began to take shape.
evt-ede-painted-tomb: The painted wall of Tomb 100 at Hierakonpolis — Egypt's oldest known tomb murals, with boats, hunters and beasts on a tawny ground.
evt-ede-predynastic-faience: A heap of glazed faience beads — the bright blue-green glassy paste the Egyptians invented and never stopped making.
evt-ede-boat-building: A reed boat painted on the wall of Hierakonpolis Tomb 100 — a glimpse of the Nile craft that carried predynastic Egypt's goods and gods.
evt-ede-irrigation-systems: The Scorpion macehead shows the king himself swinging a hoe to cut a canal — royal power tied from the start to controlling the Nile's water.
evt-ede-predynastic-goldwork: A figure sheathed in hammered gold leaf from Tell el-Farkha — some of the earliest goldwork in Egypt, its eyes inlaid in blue.
evt-ede-abydos-royal-cemetery: Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos, the desert valley the first kings chose for their tombs — a royal burial ground that endured for centuries.
evt-ede-tomb-u-j: Bone and ivory tags from Tomb U-j at Abydos, scratched with some of the earliest signs in Egypt — writing at the very moment it was born.
evt-ede-earliest-hieroglyphs: A late-predynastic palette carved with early hieroglyphic signs in relief — picture-writing taking firm hold just before the dynasties begin.
evt-ede-cosmetic-palettes: The Two Dogs Palette from Hierakonpolis — a ceremonial cosmetic palette crowded with real and fantastic beasts around its central grinding circle.
evt-ede-gebel-el-arak-knife: The Gebel el-Arak Knife, both faces shown — its ivory handle carved with a battle and a Mesopotamian-style hero, proof of early contact across the deserts.
evt-ede-upper-lower-conflict: The Hunters Palette shows a band of armed men closing on their prey — the martial imagery of an age when Upper and Lower Egypt were fighting toward one crown.
evt-ede-narmer-palette: The Narmer Palette, both faces — the carved slate that announces Egypt's unification, with the king smiting an enemy on one side and parading in triumph on the other.
evt-ede-unification: Narmer in the white crown of Upper Egypt raises his mace over a kneeling foe — the image traditionally read as the moment the Two Lands became one.
evt-ede-scorpion-king: A detail of the Scorpion macehead showing King Scorpion in the tall white crown, the scorpion sign floating before his face.
evt-ede-serekh: A serekh — the falcon-topped palace-facade frame that held a king's name, the earliest way Egypt wrote royalty.
evt-ede-memphis-founded: The ruins of Memphis amid Nile-flooded fields — little remains of the city founded to rule the newly united Two Lands from where Upper meets Lower Egypt.
evt-ede-hor-aha: A glazed vessel fragment bearing the name of Hor-Aha — the king usually counted as the founder of Egypt's First Dynasty.
evt-ede-djer: A cylinder-seal impression naming King Djer, whose Abydos tomb was ringed by hundreds of sacrificed retainers buried to serve him in death.
evt-ede-royal-tombs-abydos: A plan of the royal tombs at Umm el-Qa'ab, Abydos — the clustered mud-brick burials of the First Dynasty kings and their followers.
evt-ede-djet: The funerary stela of King Djet — a serpent coiled inside the palace frame spells his name, earning him the title the Serpent King.
evt-ede-merneith: The stela of Merneith from Abydos — a queen who ruled in her own right, the first known female head of state in Egypt.
evt-ede-den: A carved face long associated with King Den, whose long reign marks the high point of the First Dynasty.
evt-ede-heb-sed: A statuette of a king enthroned in the tight Sed-festival robe with the Horus falcon behind him — the jubilee rite that renewed a pharaoh's power.
evt-ede-anedjib-semerkhet: An incised figure of King Anedjib in the white crown — one of the last and shakiest rulers of the troubled late First Dynasty.
evt-ede-saqqara-mastabas: The desert plateau of Saqqara, where the great mud-brick mastaba tombs of the early dynasties stood — later crowned by Djoser's Step Pyramid seen here.
evt-ede-byblos-trade: The coastal town of Byblos in Lebanon — the port that shipped prized cedar timber to a near-treeless Egypt from the earliest dynasties.
evt-ede-hetepsekhemwy: A stone vessel inscribed with the name of Hetepsekhemwy, the king who opened Egypt's Second Dynasty.
evt-ede-nynetjer: A small seated statue of King Nynetjer in the white crown — a Second Dynasty ruler remembered for an unusually long reign.
evt-ede-peribsen: The stela of Peribsen, topped not by the Horus falcon but by the Seth animal — a startling break in royal tradition during a divided Second Dynasty.
evt-ede-khasekhemwy: A seated statue of Khasekhemwy in the white crown — the king who put down rebellion and reunited Egypt at the close of the Second Dynasty.
evt-ede-nimaathap: A seal impression naming Queen Nimaathap, the royal mother whose line bridged the Second Dynasty and the Old Kingdom to come.
evt-ede-gisr-el-mudir: A plan of Saqqara marking the Great Enclosure of Gisr el-Mudir — a massive early stone wall that may be a forerunner of the pyramid complexes.
evt-lu-xiufu: A line-drawing portrait of Lu Xiufu, the Song minister who strapped the boy emperor to his back and leapt into the sea rather than surrender to the Mongols.
evt-battle-yamen: The Yamen battlefield memorial gate in Guangdong, marking the 1279 sea fight where the Southern Song's last fleet was wiped out.
evt-yuan-kublai-khan: The famous court portrait of Kublai Khan, Genghis's grandson and the founder of the Yuan dynasty in China.
evt-yuan-proclaimed: The Yuan empire around 1290, the Mongol-ruled China that Kublai proclaimed in 1271 with its capital at Khanbaliq.
evt-siege-xiangyang: A Chinese diagram of a multi-shot catapult, the kind of siege artillery (later joined by Muslim counterweight trebuchets) that finally cracked Xiangyang's walls.
evt-southern-song-loyalists: A portrait of Wen Tianxiang, the Song loyalist who kept resisting the Mongols and chose execution over serving the Yuan.
evt-khanbaliq: A plan of Khanbaliq (Cambaluc), Kublai's grand grid-planned capital on the site of modern Beijing.
evt-grand-canal-extension: The Grand Canal's routes, including the new northern stretch the Yuan dug to haul grain straight to Khanbaliq.
evt-examination-suspended: The cramped cells of the imperial examination hall in Beijing — the very system the Mongols shut down for decades, slamming the door on the Chinese scholar class.
evt-tibetan-buddhism-state: Sakya Monastery in Tibet, seat of the Sakya school whose lamas became the Yuan court's spiritual heavyweights.
evt-phagpa-script: A gold imperial passport (paizi) carrying the new Phags-pa script, the universal alphabet Kublai commissioned to write every language of his empire.
evt-yuan-architecture: A carved celadon model of a Yuan-era pavilion, showing off the period's airy, curved-timber building style.
evt-temur-oljeitu: The court portrait of Temür Öljeitü, Kublai's grandson who took the throne in 1294 and tried to hold the empire steady.
evt-japan-invasion-1274: A scene from the Mongol Invasion Scrolls: Mongol horsemen clash with a lone Japanese samurai during the 1274 landing.
evt-japan-invasion-1281: Japanese warriors storm a Mongol ship in the scrolls of Takezaki Suenaga, depicting the far larger 1281 seaborne invasion.
evt-kamikaze: A painting of the Mongol fleet being smashed apart in a typhoon — the 'divine wind' (kamikaze) the Japanese credited with saving them twice.
evt-koryo-vassal: The Yuan realm in 1294 with Goryeo Korea (hatched) attached as a loyal vassal kingdom.
evt-marco-polo: Marco Polo decked out in 'Tartar' costume — the Venetian who claimed years of service at Kublai Khan's court.
evt-rabban-sauma: The route of Rabban Bar Sauma, the Beijing-born monk who traveled all the way to Rome and Paris as a Mongol envoy.
evt-john-montecorvino: A medieval manuscript of the letters of John of Montecorvino, the friar who built the first Catholic mission in Khanbaliq.
evt-pax-mongolica-trade: A caravan crossing Asia in the Catalan Atlas — the kind of long-haul trade the Mongol peace made safe from China to the Mediterranean.
evt-yam-postal-system: A gold paizi, the metal pass that let a rider use the Yam relay stations to gallop messages clear across the empire.
evt-yuan-zaju-drama: A depiction of Yuan-era performers, capturing the golden age of zaju, the variety drama that boomed under Mongol rule.
evt-guan-hanqing: A Yuan-dynasty wall painting of a theatrical troupe — the world that the great playwright Guan Hanqing wrote for.
evt-wang-shifu-romance: A color woodblock illustration to The Romance of the Western Chamber, Wang Shifu's hit Yuan love story.
evt-zhao-mengfu: A portrait of Zhao Mengfu, the Song prince who served the Yuan and became its towering master of painting and calligraphy.
evt-huang-gongwang: A portrait of Huang Gongwang, one of the Four Masters whose freewheeling landscapes defined Yuan literati painting.
evt-zheng-sixiao: Gong Kai's 'Emaciated Horse,' a starved noble steed standing in for loyal Song scholars left to wither under Mongol rule.
evt-quanzhou-port: Quanzhou's medieval Luoyang Bridge — a survivor from the era when this port was one of the busiest trade harbors on earth.
evt-ibn-battuta-china: A 19th-century illustration of the Moroccan globetrotter Ibn Battuta, who reached Yuan China at the tail end of his epic travels.
evt-paper-money-yuan: A Yuan paper banknote beside its printing plate — the world's first empire-wide paper currency, which astonished Marco Polo.
evt-blue-and-white-porcelain: A Yuan blue-and-white vase from Jingdezhen, the cobalt-painted porcelain that became China's most famous export.
evt-jamal-al-din-ilkhanate: A Persian astrolabe — the kind of instrument the Muslim astronomers Kublai recruited brought to the observatory at Khanbaliq.
evt-yuan-astronomy: A statue of Guo Shoujing, the Yuan astronomer-engineer whose calendar pinned the year to within seconds of the true value.
evt-quanzhou-revolt: A map of the Xinghua region during the Ispah Rebellion, the bloody revolt of foreign garrison troops that tore through Quanzhou.
evt-yuan-succession-chaos: The Mongol Empire split into rival khanates — the kind of fracturing mirrored at Khanbaliq, where emperors rose and fell in a blur after Kublai.
evt-yellow-river-floods: Ma Yuan's painting of the Yellow River bursting its banks — the disaster that, in 1344, drowned the countryside and helped doom the Yuan.
evt-mongol-army-decay: A Yuan iron helmet — relic of the once-feared Mongol war machine that had gone soft and rusty by the dynasty's final decades.
evt-white-lotus-society: A painting tied to the White Lotus Society, the secret Buddhist sect whose millenarian preaching lit the fuse on anti-Yuan revolt.
evt-red-turban-rebellions: A map of the rebel warlords carving up China at the end of the Yuan, the chaos out of which the Red Turbans rose.
evt-zhu-yuanzhang: The seated court portrait of Zhu Yuanzhang — the peasant-turned-rebel who toppled the Mongols and founded the Ming as the Hongwu Emperor.
evt-zhang-shicheng: A map of the Lake Poyang theater, where Zhu Yuanzhang crushed his great rival warlord in the decisive naval battle of 1363.
evt-toghon-temur: A portrait of Toghon Temür, the last Yuan emperor, who fled north as the Ming armies closed in on his capital.
evt-ming-founded: The Ming empire that rose from the Yuan's ashes, founded in 1368 with the Mongols driven back to the steppe.
evt-naval-rice-transport: The excavated hull of a 13th-century Chinese seagoing junk raised from Quanzhou Bay — the kind of oceangoing ship the Yuan loaded with grain to haul rice by sea up the coast to the capital.
evt-semu-administration: A Yuan silk painting of a Mongol rider accompanied by a mounted administrator — the foreign Semu officials the Mongols planted above the Chinese to run the empire's books.
evt-yuan-cosmopolitan-court: A detail of Empress Chabi from Liu Guandao's Yuan court hunting scroll — a glimpse of Kublai's mixed, cosmopolitan retinue of Mongols, Chinese, and foreign servants riding out together.
evt-ede-earliest-copper: A copper harpoon tip from a grave at Naqada — one of the earliest worked-metal objects in Egypt, hammered from cold copper before true smelting.
evt-ede-predynastic-linen: The Tarkhan Dress, woven from predynastic linen — the oldest surviving garment in the world, proof of how fine Egypt's early weaving had already become.
evt-ede-cities-of-dead: A predynastic body naturally dried in the hot desert sand, still curled among its pottery — the kind of grave that filled Egypt's earliest cemeteries of the dead.
evt-ede-hierakonpolis-rise: Early excavations at Kom el-Ahmar — the mound that is ancient Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), the southern town that grew into Upper Egypt's first great power.
evt-ede-earliest-temples: A 19th-century drawing of the brick revetment of the early temple at Hierakonpolis — the mud-brick footing of one of Egypt's oldest known shrines.
evt-ede-lapis-lazuli-trade: A lump of raw lapis lazuli — a deep-blue stone Egypt could only get from Afghanistan, carried thousands of miles along the trade routes of the predynastic age.
evt-oke-djoser: Painted limestone statue of Djoser from his Saqqara complex — the oldest known life-size royal statue from Egypt.
evt-oke-imhotep: Bronze statuette of Imhotep, Djoser's architect, seated with an open papyrus on his lap — by which point Egypt had turned him into a god of wisdom.
evt-oke-step-pyramid: Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, six stacked mastabas rising from the desert — the world's first monument built entirely of dressed stone.
evt-oke-stone-vessel-production: A case of carved stone vessels in alabaster, granite, and breccia — the kind of painstaking hard-stone work Egyptian craftsmen mass-produced for the tombs.
evt-oke-sekhemkhet-pyramid: Line drawings of King Sekhemkhet, Djoser's short-reigning successor whose own step pyramid at Saqqara was never finished and lay buried for millennia.
evt-oke-nilometer: A stone nilometer's stepped shaft and central measuring column — the device by which Egypt gauged each year's flood and set the taxes to match.
evt-oke-sed-festival: Alabaster statuette of a king kneeling in his Sed-festival robe, the falcon-god Horus perched behind him — the jubilee meant to renew a pharaoh's powers.
evt-oke-sneferu: Statue of Sneferu, the first king of the Fourth Dynasty and the most prolific pyramid-builder Egypt ever produced.
evt-oke-meidum-pyramid: The collapsed Meidum pyramid, its core tower rising from a heap of its own fallen casing — an early Sneferu project that did not hold together.
evt-oke-bent-pyramid: Sneferu's Bent Pyramid at Dahshur, whose sides change angle partway up — the moment the builders lost their nerve about a too-steep slope.
evt-oke-red-pyramid: Sneferu's Red Pyramid at Dahshur, the first successful true smooth-sided pyramid and the template for Giza.
evt-oke-khufu: The three-inch ivory statuette of Khufu — the only known likeness of the king who built the largest pyramid on Earth.
evt-oke-great-pyramid: Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza, for nearly four thousand years the tallest structure humans had ever built.
evt-oke-hemiunu: Seated limestone statue of Hemiunu, Khufu's vizier and the man widely credited with overseeing the Great Pyramid's construction.
evt-oke-giza-workers-village: The Giza pyramids — built and serviced by a permanent town of paid laborers, bakers, and brewers whose ruins lie just to the south.
evt-oke-bread-beer-economy: A painted wooden tomb model of workers grinding grain and tending bread molds — the bread-and-beer rations that paid Egypt's laborers.
evt-oke-khufu-ship: Khufu's reassembled cedar solar barque, found dismantled in a pit beside the Great Pyramid and pieced back together plank by plank.
evt-oke-papyrus: A sheet of papyrus covered in cursive script — the cheap, portable writing material that ran Egypt's paperwork-heavy bureaucracy.
evt-oke-hieratic: A page of flowing hieratic script — the everyday cursive shorthand scribes wrote with reed pens, far faster than carving full hieroglyphs.
evt-oke-khafre: The diorite enthroned statue of Khafre, builder of the second Giza pyramid, with the falcon Horus sheltering the back of his head.
evt-oke-sphinx: The Great Sphinx at Giza, a recumbent lion with a king's face, carved from the bedrock beside Khafre's causeway.
evt-oke-menkaure: Greywacke statue of Menkaure, builder of the smallest of the three Giza pyramids.
evt-oke-giza-causeway-valley-temple: The colossal granite blocks of Khafre's Valley Temple wall — the riverside terminus of the causeway that linked the Nile to the pyramid.
evt-oke-khamerernebty-ii: Close view of Queen Khamerernebty II from the famous greywacke dyad in which she stands beside her husband Menkaure.
evt-oke-meresankh-iii: Statue group of Queen Meresankh III with her mother Hetepheres II, a royal woman whose painted Giza tomb survives nearly intact.
evt-oke-userkaf: Head of Userkaf, founder of the Fifth Dynasty and the first king to build a temple to the sun-god as a state project.
evt-oke-sun-temples: Reconstruction drawing of a Fifth-Dynasty sun temple at Abu Gorab, built around a squat obelisk and an open-air altar to Ra.
evt-oke-sahure: Gneiss statue of King Sahure seated beside a personified nome god — a Fifth-Dynasty ruler famous for his far-flung trading fleets.
evt-oke-punt-expedition: Relief drawing of the chief of Punt and his family greeting Egyptian traders — the distant southern land Egypt sailed to for incense, gold, and exotica.
evt-oke-abusir-pyramids: The eroded mudbrick-cored pyramids of Abusir, the Fifth Dynasty's royal cemetery between Giza and Saqqara.
evt-oke-ptahhotep: The Prisse Papyrus, carrying the Maxims of Ptahhotep — a vizier's manual of advice on how to live and rise in the world.
evt-oke-djedkare-isesi: The ruined pyramid of Djedkare Isesi at South Saqqara, the long-reigning Fifth-Dynasty king who reshaped the royal administration.
evt-oke-palermo-stone: The Palermo Stone, a black basalt slab inscribed year by year with Egypt's earliest kings and their flood heights — one of our oldest historical records.
evt-oke-unas: The weathered pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, last king of the Fifth Dynasty and the first to inscribe his burial chamber with spells.
evt-oke-pyramid-texts: Columns of carved spells inside Unas's burial chamber — the Pyramid Texts, the oldest body of religious writing yet found.
evt-oke-teti: Standing statue of Teti, founder of the Sixth Dynasty, whose reign opened the last great chapter of the Old Kingdom.
evt-oke-pepi-i: The hammered copper statue of Pepi I from Hierakonpolis — the earliest known large metal statue from anywhere in the world.
evt-oke-weni: The long inscribed slab from Weni's tomb at Abydos, in which the official narrates his rise from minor clerk to general and governor.
evt-oke-harkhuf: Relief of an official from the Aswan cliff tombs — the burial ground of explorers like Harkhuf, who led caravans deep into Nubia.
evt-oke-pepi-ii: Alabaster statuette of the boy-king Pepi II seated on the lap of his mother Ankhnesmeryre II — he took the throne as a child and reigned for an astonishing span.
evt-oke-old-kingdom-collapse: A provincial funerary stele of the First Intermediate Period, the fragmented era of local rulers that followed the Old Kingdom's collapse.
evt-oke-famine-relief: Map of the 4.2-kiloyear drought event, the abrupt climate downturn whose feeble Nile floods helped starve and break the Old Kingdom.
evt-oke-herakleopolis-dynasty: A seal bearing the cartouche of a King Khety — the line of Herakleopolitan rulers who claimed the throne of a divided Egypt.
evt-oke-theban-rise: The cliffs of Deir el-Bahari at Thebes, the southern power base from which a new line of kings would challenge the north.
evt-oke-ankhtifi: Tomb relief of Ankhtifi, the swaggering warlord of Mo'alla who boasted of feeding his people through famine while his neighbors starved.
evt-oke-ipuwer: The Ipuwer Papyrus, a bleak poem of a world turned upside down — long read as a literary echo of the Old Kingdom's collapse.
evt-oke-coffin-texts: The painted interior of a wooden coffin covered in spells — the Coffin Texts, which democratized the afterlife once reserved for kings.
evt-oke-dialogue-man-soul: The Berlin papyrus of the Dispute Between a Man and His Ba — a despairing soul arguing with itself over whether life is worth living.
evt-oke-merikare: A scribe's palette inscribed with the name Merikare — the king to whom a Herakleopolitan father addressed his hard-won lessons in ruling.
evt-oke-basin-irrigation: A tomb painting of a man working a shaduf, the counterweighted lever Egyptians used to lift Nile water into their fields and basins.
evt-oke-mentuhotep-ii: The black-painted seated statue of Mentuhotep II, the Theban king who crushed the north and reunited Egypt after generations of division.
evt-oke-mortuary-temple-mentuhotep: The ruined terraces of Mentuhotep II's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, the bold new design later copied next door by Hatshepsut.
evt-oke-calendar: A carved temple calendar listing festivals month by month — Egypt's 365-day civil year was one of the ancient world's great timekeeping achievements.
evt-oke-sinai-mining: An inscribed stela standing among the ruins at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai, where Egyptian expeditions hacked turquoise and copper from the desert.
evt-mhe-vertical-archipelago: An Andean axe-money blank, the kind of portable metal that moved between ecological zones in the vertical-archipelago trade.
evt-mhe-khipu-origins: A khipu, the knotted-cord recording device the Andes used in place of writing.
evt-mhe-gateway-of-sun: The Gateway of the Sun at Tiwanaku, carved from a single block of stone.
evt-mhe-pikillaqta: A street running through Pikillaqta, the rigidly gridded Wari city southeast of Cusco.
evt-mhe-bennett-monolith: The towering Bennett Monolith, Tiwanaku's largest carved stone figure.
evt-mhe-tiwanaku-city: The sprawling monumental core of Tiwanaku, seen from above on the Bolivian altiplano.
evt-mhe-suka-kollu: A reconstructed raised field (waru waru), the ridge-and-canal system that let crops survive altiplano frosts.
evt-mhe-akapana: The stepped stone terracing of Tiwanaku's monumental platforms.
evt-mhe-kalasasaya: The walled Kalasasaya enclosure at Tiwanaku, its perimeter studded with upright stone pillars.
evt-mhe-tiwanaku-religion: The Staff God carved at the center of the Gateway of the Sun, the era's signature deity.
evt-mhe-pumapunku: The scattered, precisely cut stone blocks of the Pumapunku platform at Tiwanaku.
evt-mhe-pumapunku-pseudoscience: A precise cross-shaped recess cut into Pumapunku stone, the machine-clean carving that fuels modern pseudoscientific claims.
evt-mhe-llama-caravans: Llamas grazing below the Andean peaks, the pack animals that carried Tiwanaku and Wari goods across the highlands.
evt-mhe-wari-founded: A carved stone monolith from Wari near Ayacucho, the empire's highland capital.
evt-mhe-conchopata: A painted Wari ceramic vessel of the kind smashed in ritual offerings at Conchopata.
evt-mhe-viracochapampa: The unfinished stone walls of Viracochapampa, a Wari provincial center left incomplete.
evt-mhe-cajamarquilla: The entrance marker for the Cajamarquilla archaeological site near Lima.
evt-mhe-women-weavers-status: A finely woven Wari tunic, the kind of textile produced by the empire's high-status weavers.
evt-mhe-inca-build-on-wari: A colonial portrait of Manco Capac, first Inca, whose empire inherited Wari roads and administration.
evt-mhe-aymara-language: A map of the Aymara-speaking zone around Lake Titicaca and the southern altiplano.
evt-mhe-tello-discovery: Julio C. Tello, the Peruvian archaeologist who helped frame the modern Wari question.
evt-mhe-vilca-snuff: A carved Andean snuff tray used to inhale hallucinogenic vilca powder in ritual.
evt-mhe-cerro-baul: Cerro Baul, the flat-topped mesa the Wari fortified as a colony deep in Tiwanaku territory.
evt-mhe-tiwanaku-colonies: Monumental Tiwanaku stonework, the cultural signature its colonists carried into distant valleys.
evt-mhe-moquegua-coexistence: The Moquegua valley town today, where Wari and Tiwanaku colonists once lived side by side.
evt-mhe-pachacamac-wari: The coastal pilgrimage center of Pachacamac, drawn into the Wari sphere.
evt-mhe-cerro-baul-brewery: The summit of Cerro Baul, where the Wari ran a large hilltop brewery.
evt-mhe-cerro-baul-excavation: Visitors climbing the steep flanks of Cerro Baul, the site of decades of Wari excavation.
evt-mhe-qollqa-storehouses: Stone storehouse foundations of the kind the Andes used to stockpile surplus food.
evt-mhe-wari-textile: A Wari tunic densely woven with stylized figures, among the finest textiles of the ancient Andes.
evt-mhe-ushnu-platforms: A stepped ceremonial platform (ushnu) of the kind later Andean states built for ritual.
evt-mhe-drought-900: The Quelccaya ice cap, whose layered ice records the multi-decade drought that struck the Andes around 900.
evt-mhe-wari-abandonment: An exposed tomb among the ruins of Wari, the capital eventually left empty.
evt-mhe-tiwanaku-abandonment: The Ponce-style Fraile Monolith standing alone amid the deserted ruins of Tiwanaku.
evt-mhe-late-intermediate-fragmentation: A map of the patchwork of regional polities that filled the Andes after Wari and Tiwanaku fell.
evt-mhe-chimu-rises: Adobe wall reliefs at Chan Chan, capital of the Chimu who inherited the Wari coast.
evt-mhe-cieza-de-leon: The 1553 title page of Pedro Cieza de Leon's chronicle, our earliest written account of Tiwanaku.
evt-mhe-bandelier-1894: Adolph Bandelier, who excavated in the Lake Titicaca region in the 1890s.
evt-mhe-wari-grid-cities: The terraced ruins of the Wari capital near Ayacucho, the empire that pioneered planned grid cities.
evt-mhe-honcopampa: The stone structures of Honcopampa set against the snowcapped peaks of the Callejon de Huaylas.
evt-mhe-wari-elite-burials: The excavated tomb chambers of El Castillo de Huarmey, the unlooted resting place of Wari noblewomen.
evt-arthashastra: A palm-leaf manuscript of the Arthashastra in Grantha script, the treatise on statecraft attributed to Chanakya.
evt-chandragupta-founding: A modern statue of Chandragupta Maurya, the soldier who toppled the Nandas and founded India's first great empire.
evt-chanakya: An artist's depiction of Chanakya, the wily Brahmin strategist who masterminded Chandragupta's rise.
evt-nanda-dynasty: The Nanda realm around 325 BCE, the wealthy Magadhan power Chandragupta would overthrow.
evt-pataliputra-capital: Excavated stumps of the great pillared hall at Kumrahar, all that survives of the Maurya capital Pataliputra.
evt-indica-megasthenes: The excavated wooden palisade at Bulandi Bagh - the giant timber wall around Pataliputra that Megasthenes marveled at in his Indica.
evt-defeat-seleucus: The eastern satrapies Seleucus ceded to Chandragupta after their war, settled with a treaty and 500 war elephants.
evt-battle-ipsus: The Battle of Ipsus, where Seleucus deployed the war elephants he had gained from the Mauryas to crush Antigonus.
evt-punch-marked-coins: Silver punch-marked karshapana coins, the stamped currency that oiled the Maurya economy.
evt-maurya-metallurgy: The watered pattern of wootz steel, the prized high-carbon crucible steel that South Asian smiths pioneered.
evt-chandragupta-jainism: Chandragupta with the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu, whom he followed south after renouncing his throne for Jainism.
evt-taxila-university: The ruins of Taxila, the northwestern city renowned as a great center of learning.
evt-maurya-bureaucracy: A Maurya-era terracotta figure from Patna, a glimpse of the people the empire's vast bureaucracy governed.
evt-state-monopolies: A hoard of mostly Mauryan silver coins, the wealth flowing from state monopolies over mines, salt, and liquor.
evt-maurya-legal-system: A page of the Arthashastra, whose detailed code of fines and punishments framed the Maurya legal system.
evt-bindusara: A silver karshapana struck under Bindusara, the son of Chandragupta who held the empire together for a quarter-century.
evt-deccan-campaign: Magadha's heartland before its great southward expansion, the campaigns that pushed Maurya power into the Deccan.
evt-bindusara-ajivikas: The Visvakarma cave at Barabar, one of the rock-cut sanctuaries the Mauryas gave to the Ajivika ascetics.
evt-succession-crisis: A carved panel at Kanaganahalli labeled with Ashoka's name - among the few ancient portraits of the prince who seized the throne.
evt-ashoka-ujjain: Ujjain, the western provincial capital the young prince Ashoka governed before becoming emperor.
evt-kalinga-war: The peace pagoda at Dhauli in Kalinga, near the battlefield whose carnage turned Ashoka against war.
evt-ashoka-converts: A Sanchi gateway relief showing Ashoka, now a Buddhist devotee, journeying to venerate a stupa.
evt-rock-edicts: The Maski rock edict, one of Ashoka's proclamations carved on stone - and the one that names him outright as Ashoka.
evt-brahmi-script: Brahmi lettering on an Ashokan pillar at Sarnath, the script the edicts standardized across the empire.
evt-kharosthi-script: Ashoka's first edict at Shahbazgarhi cut in Kharosthi, the right-to-left script of the empire's northwest.
evt-religious-tolerance-edict: Girnar's twelfth major rock edict, in which Ashoka calls for honoring all religious sects, not just one's own.
evt-animal-welfare-edicts: Girnar's first major rock edict, which bans animal sacrifice and curbs the slaughter of living creatures.
evt-dhamma-mahamatras: An Ashokan pillar inscription of the kind that announced his dhamma officers, the magistrates sent out to spread moral law.
evt-pillar-edicts: The Delhi-Topra pillar of Ashoka, one of the tall polished monoliths inscribed with his pillar edicts.
evt-sanchi-stupa: The Great Stupa at Sanchi, the great dome of Buddhist devotion that Ashoka first raised.
evt-third-buddhist-council: A temple mural of Ashoka presiding over the Third Buddhist Council, which purged the order and settled doctrine.
evt-pali-canon: A palm-leaf set of the Tipitaka, the threefold Pali canon of Buddhist scripture compiled in this era.
evt-mahinda-sri-lanka: A statue of the monk Mahinda, Ashoka's son, who carried Buddhism across the sea to Sri Lanka.
evt-sanghamitta: A mural of the nun Sanghamitta bearing a sapling of the Bodhi tree to Sri Lanka.
evt-gandhara-school: A standing Gandhara Buddha, its Greek-style drapery the hallmark of the northwest's Greco-Buddhist art.
evt-barabar-caves: The arched, mirror-polished doorway of the Lomas Rishi cave at Barabar, India's oldest surviving rock-cut sanctuary.
evt-lumbini-pillar: Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini, whose inscription marks the Buddha's birthplace and exempted the village from tax.
evt-dasharatha: The dedication inscription of Dasharatha Maurya above the Gopika cave at Nagarjuni, granted to the Ajivikas.
evt-lion-capital: The Lion Capital of Ashoka from Sarnath, four lions back-to-back atop a polished sandstone shaft.
evt-ashoka-chakra: The Sarnath capital crowned by the Dharma wheel - the Ashoka Chakra that now sits at the center of India's flag.
evt-chunar-sandstone: A single-lion capital cut from Chunar sandstone, the buff stone quarried for nearly all of Ashoka's pillars.
evt-prinsep-brahmi: James Prinsep, the colonial scholar who cracked the Brahmi script in 1837 and gave Ashoka's edicts a voice.
evt-maurya-polish: The glassy mirror-polished granite walls of the Sudama cave, the signature Maurya stone finish.
evt-decline-fragmentation: The Maurya Empire at its height around 250 BCE - the unity that splintered within decades of Ashoka's death.
evt-northwest-incursion: A coin portrait of Demetrius I of Bactria wearing an elephant-scalp headdress, the Greek king who pushed into the northwest.
evt-pushyamitra-coup: An inscription naming Pushyamitra Shunga, the general who murdered the last Maurya and seized the throne.
evt-shunga-dynasty: A reconstruction of the Great Stupa as enlarged under the Shungas, the dynasty that replaced the Mauryas.
evt-brihadratha: An Ashokan pillar at Vaishali, a relic of the empire that ended with the murder of its last ruler, Brihadratha.
evt-royal-highway: The route of the Grand Trunk Road, the modern descendant of the ancient Uttarapatha that the Mauryas built across the north.
evt-arthashastra-rediscovery: The Oriental Research Institute in Mysore, where a palm-leaf copy of the long-lost Arthashastra surfaced in 1905.
evt-melgar-discovery: San Lorenzo Colossal Head 2, the kind of multi-ton basalt portrait whose 1862 discovery first hinted that a forgotten civilization had carved the Gulf coast.
evt-stirling-excavations: Matthew Stirling and his wife Marion in the field in Veracruz, where their excavations pulled the Olmec out of legend and into the archaeological record.
evt-rubber-balls: A solid rubber ball beside a stone hand-guard, the gear of a game the Olmec helped invent from the Gulf lowlands' latex trees.
evt-maize-cultivation: A milpa, the maize-beans-squash field system that fed the Olmec and every Mesoamerican civilization after them.
evt-san-lorenzo-founded: Excavations at San Lorenzo's so-called Red Palace, an elite compound at the Olmec's first great center.
evt-la-venta-rises: The great earthen mound at La Venta, the swamp-island capital that took over after San Lorenzo's fall.
evt-olmec-wrestling: The Wrestler, a basalt figure caught mid-crouch that ranks among the most lifelike sculptures the Olmec left behind.
evt-colossal-heads-san-lorenzo: San Lorenzo Monument 4, one of the helmeted colossal heads quarried, hauled, and carved at the Olmec's first capital.
evt-olmec-shaman-rulers: A helmeted seated figure from San Lorenzo, the sort of part-human, part-beast image tied to the Olmec's shaman-rulers.
evt-san-lorenzo-monument14: An Olmec table-top throne with a ruler emerging from its niche, the same form as San Lorenzo's Monument 14.
evt-san-lorenzo-monument-destruction: San Lorenzo Monument 3, one of the great sculptures defaced and buried when the city's order collapsed.
evt-nahual-concept: A later Mesoamerican codex page showing humans paired with animal spirits, the nahual idea whose roots reach back to the Olmec.
evt-la-cobata-head: The La Cobata head on display at Santiago Tuxtla, the largest and most roughly finished of the Olmec colossal heads.
evt-basalt-transport: San Lorenzo Colossal Head 8, carved from basalt dragged dozens of miles from the Tuxtla Mountains without wheels or draft animals.
evt-throne-head-recycling: A weathered La Venta head whose stone, like several others, may have begun life as a ruler's throne before being recut.
evt-mesoamerican-ballgame: A clay figurine of a ballplayer in protective gear, frozen in the game the Olmec set in motion across Mesoamerica.
evt-olmec-feathered-serpent: La Venta Stela 19, the earliest known image of a feathered serpent, coiled around a seated figure.
evt-olmec-bloodletting: An Olmec stone implement of the kind used to draw blood in the bloodletting rites that ran through Mesoamerican religion.
evt-juxtlahuaca-cave: A painted figure deep inside Juxtlahuaca cave, among the oldest surviving Olmec wall paintings.
evt-oxtotitlan-cave: A polychrome mural at Oxtotitlán cave in Guerrero, where Olmec-style painting survives in vivid color.
evt-jade-trade: An Olmec jade mask, carved from greenstone the Olmec imported across hundreds of miles from the Motagua valley.
evt-cacao-cultivation: A split cacao pod showing the seeds, processed into the bitter chocolate drink the Olmec were among the first to brew.
evt-tlatilco-olmec: The Tlatilco Acrobat, a ceramic figure from a highland village steeped in Olmec style far from the Gulf coast.
evt-chalcatzingo: The El Rey relief at Chalcatzingo, where a ruler sits inside a cave-mouth breathing scrolls of rain, carved in pure Olmec idiom.
evt-olmec-influence-spreads: The Lord of Las Limas, a greenstone figure cradling a limp were-jaguar infant, an image echoed wherever Olmec influence reached.
evt-olmec-trade-networks: The Kunz Axe, a polished jade celt of the type the Olmec traded and offered across Mesoamerica.
evt-great-pyramid-la-venta: The Great Pyramid of La Venta, a roughly 100-foot earthen mound that anchored the city's ceremonial core.
evt-la-venta-complex-a: Complex A at La Venta, the walled precinct where the Olmec buried lavish offerings beneath the ground.
evt-la-venta-mosaic: A serpentine mosaic pavement from La Venta, a stylized face laid in green stone and then deliberately buried.
evt-massive-offerings: Offering 4 from La Venta, a tableau of jade and greenstone figurines arranged around upright celts, then sealed underground.
evt-tomb-of-columns: The basalt-column tomb from La Venta, a roofed chamber built from hauled stone pillars for a high-ranking burial.
evt-la-venta-stela1: La Venta Stela 1, a standing figure carved in low relief on a basalt slab at the Olmec capital.
evt-la-venta-decline: An Olmec monument from La Venta, now relocated to a park-museum after the site itself was abandoned around 400 BC.
evt-cascajal-block: The glyphs of the Cascajal Block, the strongest candidate for the earliest writing in the Americas.
evt-zapotec-script: Carved glyphs at Monte Albán, where the neighboring Zapotec developed one of Mesoamerica's first true scripts.
evt-mesoamerican-calendar: Monte Albán Stelae 12 and 13, early calendrical inscriptions in the day-and-month system the Olmec helped seed.
evt-stela-c-tres-zapotes: Stela C from Tres Zapotes, its bar-and-dot Long Count date among the oldest such inscriptions known.
evt-isthmian-script: The La Mojarra stela, packed with columns of the still-undeciphered Isthmian script.
evt-tres-zapotes: A ceramic vessel from Tres Zapotes, the Gulf center that outlasted San Lorenzo and La Venta into the epi-Olmec era.
evt-epi-olmec: The Harvester Mountain Lord of La Mojarra, a richly costumed ruler in the epi-Olmec style that followed the classic Olmec.
evt-tuxtla-statuette: The Tuxtla Statuette, a jade duck-billed figure incised with an early epi-Olmec Long Count date and Isthmian text.
evt-cerro-de-las-mesas: Cerro de las Mesas Stela 6, from the late Gulf-coast center whose buried jade cache numbered in the hundreds.
evt-mother-culture-debate: An Olmec masterwork in stone, the kind of achievement that fuels the debate over whether the Olmec were Mesoamerica's mother culture.
evt-covarrubias-olmec-art: Miguel Covarrubias, the artist-scholar who traced Olmec style across Mesoamerica and argued for its deep influence.
evt-monte-alban-rival: Monte Albán in the Oaxaca highlands, the Zapotec capital that rose as the Olmec world wound down.
evt-teotihuacan-emerges: Teotihuacán, the giant central-Mexican city that grew into Mesoamerica's next great power after the Olmec.
evt-qin-shang-yang: A modern statue of Shang Yang, the Legalist statesman who rebuilt the state of Qin from the ground up.
evt-qin-battle-changping: A map of the Battle of Changping, the bloody clash where Qin shattered the army of Zhao.
evt-qin-bai-qi: Bai Qi, the Qin general whose campaigns left a trail of annihilated enemy armies.
evt-qin-zheng-guo-canal: A map of the Zhengguo Canal, which watered the Wei valley and helped feed Qin's war machine.
evt-qin-li-mu: Li Mu of Zhao, the last great general to hold the line against Qin.
evt-qin-qin-shi-huang: Ying Zheng, the king of Qin who would crown himself Qin Shi Huang, China's First Emperor.
evt-qin-li-si: A copy of the Yishan stele in the standardized seal script attributed to Li Si, Qin's chief minister.
evt-qin-han-feizi: A statue of Han Fei, the thinker who gave Legalism its sharpest theoretical edge.
evt-qin-jing-ke: A Han-dynasty stone rubbing of Jing Ke's failed lunge at the king of Qin, the dagger flying past the pillar.
evt-qin-conquest-han: The small central state of Han, first of the six rivals Qin swallowed whole.
evt-qin-conquest-zhao: Zhao, the northern power that fought Qin hardest before it fell.
evt-qin-conquest-wei: Wei, the central state Qin drowned by diverting rivers against its capital Daliang.
evt-qin-wang-jian: Wang Jian, the cautious Qin general who led the massive army that crushed Chu.
evt-qin-conquest-chu: A lacquer painting from the southern state of Chu, the largest and last great rival Qin destroyed.
evt-qin-conquest-yan-qi: Yan, the far-northern state whose desperate assassination plot only hastened its conquest alongside Qi.
evt-qin-standardization-script: The same words in two scripts: the small seal script (right) that Qin imposed as the empire's standard.
evt-qin-standardization-weights: A banliang coin, the round bronze piece with a square hole that Qin made the empire's single currency.
evt-qin-legalist-law-code: Qin legal texts written on bamboo slips, unearthed from a magistrate's tomb at Shuihudi.
evt-qin-commandery-county-system: A map of the Qin commanderies, the appointed-administrator districts that replaced the old feudal fiefs.
evt-qin-axle-standardization: The unified Qin empire in 221 BCE, knit together by standardized roads and cart axles.
evt-qin-five-phases-cosmology: A spirit tablet naming the Five Phases — wood, fire, earth, metal, water — the cosmology Qin used to legitimize its rule.
evt-qin-great-wall: The Great Wall snaking over the mountains; Qin first linked the northern frontier walls into one barrier.
evt-qin-ling-canal: The Ling Canal, the Qin waterway that linked the Yangtze and Pearl river systems for the southern campaigns.
evt-qin-baiyue-campaigns: A map of Qin's push south of the Yangtze into the lands of the Baiyue peoples.
evt-qin-meng-jiangnü: Meng Jiangnü weeping at the Great Wall, the folk legend of a wife whose grief brought the wall down.
evt-qin-terracotta-army: The Terracotta Army in Pit 1, thousands of life-size warriors buried to guard the First Emperor.
evt-qin-mausoleum-complex: A plan of the First Emperor's vast mausoleum complex, with the burial mound, walls, and the terracotta pits.
evt-qin-mercury-tomb-technology: The forested burial mound over the First Emperor's tomb, where soil tests still detect unusually high mercury.
evt-qin-sima-qian: Sima Qian, the Han historian whose Records of the Grand Historian is our chief account of the Qin.
evt-qin-crossbow-mass-production: Bronze crossbow trigger mechanisms, the interchangeable parts Qin mass-produced to arm its armies.
evt-qin-yang-zhifa: Ranks of terracotta warriors, the buried army that farmers near Xi'an stumbled onto while digging a well in 1974.
evt-qin-burning-books: A later painting of Qin's burning of the books, with forbidden texts set alight at the foot of the steps.
evt-qin-burying-scholars: A painting of the First Emperor's purge of scholars, the grim companion to the burning of the books.
evt-qin-immortality-quest: A statue of Xu Fu, the alchemist the First Emperor sent searching the seas for an elixir of immortality.
evt-qin-xu-fu-expedition: Utagawa Kuniyoshi's print of Xu Fu's fleet setting sail east in search of the islands of the immortals.
evt-qin-mount-tai-sacrifice: The summit of Mount Tai, where the First Emperor performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices to heaven and earth.
evt-qin-lushi-chunqiu: A printed edition of the Lushi Chunqiu, the encyclopedic compendium assembled under chancellor Lu Buwei.
evt-qin-death-first-emperor: The terracotta ranks that outlived their maker; the First Emperor died on tour in 210 BCE, his death hidden for weeks.
evt-qin-qin-er-shi: Qin Er Shi, the Second Emperor whose short, manipulated reign hastened the dynasty's collapse.
evt-qin-chen-sheng-wu-guang: A map of the revolts that broke out across the empire, beginning with the Chen Sheng and Wu Guang uprising.
evt-qin-battle-julu: A map of the Battle of Julu, where Xiang Yu smashed the main Qin army and broke its grip on the rebels.
evt-qin-xiang-yu: Xiang Yu, the towering warlord of Chu who became Qin's deadliest nemesis.
evt-qin-liu-bang: Liu Bang, the commoner-turned-rebel who would outlast Xiang Yu and found the Han dynasty.
evt-qin-ziying-last-ruler: A Qin terracotta figure standing for Ziying, the last Qin ruler, who surrendered the empire after just 46 days.
evt-qin-han-xin: Han Xin, the brilliant general whose campaigns won the empire for Liu Bang.
evt-qin-battle-gaixia: A map of the Chu–Han war closing on Gaixia, where Xiang Yu was finally cornered and destroyed.
evt-qin-chu-han-contention: A painted ceramic warhorse from the era of the Chu–Han Contention, the four-year struggle for Qin's fallen empire.
evt-qin-qin-calendar: A Qin almanac on bamboo slips, its circular chart laying out the lucky and unlucky days of the reformed calendar.
evt-qin-shuihudi-bamboo-texts: Qin bamboo slips unearthed from Tomb 11 at Shuihudi in 1975, the buried administrative and legal texts of a Qin magistrate.
evt-olmec-long-count-origins: Stela 2 from Chiapa de Corzo, whose bar-and-dot inscription carries one of the oldest Long Count dates known, from the late Olmec world.
evt-qin-shang-yang-reforms: A bronze standard measure inscribed with Shang Yang's edict, the kind of uniform weights and rules his Legalist reforms imposed on Qin.
evt-qin-sichuan-conquest: The Dujiangyan irrigation works on the Min River, the engineering that turned the conquered Sichuan Basin into a Qin granary.
evt-qin-straight-road: A map tracing the Zhidao, the Straight Road Qin drove north from the capital toward the Ordos frontier.
evt-early-minoan-settlement: The Goddess of Myrtos, a quirky long-necked clay vessel from the Early Minoan settlement at Phournou Koryphi, around 2500 BC.
evt-tholos-tombs-mesara: A cutaway engraving of a beehive-shaped tholos tomb, the corbelled domed burial form the Mesara plain made its own.
evt-mochlos-settlement: The little island of Mochlos off Crete's north coast, once a thriving Early Minoan harbor and trading post.
evt-prepalatial-seals: A gold Minoan signet ring engraved with leaping animals, the kind of carved seal Cretans used to stamp their mark.
evt-peak-sanctuaries: Clay figurines and body-part offerings left at Minoan peak sanctuaries, the open-air shrines that crowned Crete's mountaintops.
evt-first-palaces: Excavated palace foundations on Crete, photographed in 1907 as the first of the great Minoan palaces came back to light.
evt-phaistos-palace: A clay offering stand modeled with dolphins and seashells from the Palace of Phaistos, around 1700 BC.
evt-malia-palace: The excavated ruins of the Minoan palace at Malia on Crete's north coast.
evt-cretan-hieroglyphs: A green stone seal carved with Cretan hieroglyphs, the island's earliest writing system.
evt-linear-a: A clay tablet incised with Linear A, the Minoan script that still defies decipherment.
evt-kamares-ware: A Kamares-ware jug swirling with white and red spirals on a dark ground, the flashy fine pottery of the palace era.
evt-phaistos-disc: The Phaistos Disc, a fired clay disc stamped in a spiral with symbols nobody has cracked.
evt-bees-pendant-malia: The gold bee pendant from Malia, two bees clutching a drop of honey, a masterpiece of Minoan goldwork.
evt-chrysolakkos-malia: An aerial view of the Chrysolakkos burial complex near Malia, a grid of stone-walled funerary rooms.
evt-thera-eruption: Santorini's flooded caldera today, the drowned crater left when the Thera volcano blew apart.
evt-puebloans-maize-cultivation: Teosinte (left), a teosinte-maize hybrid, and modern maize, showing the slow selection that turned a wild grass into the Southwest's staple crop.
evt-puebloans-atlatl-use: A sequence showing how the atlatl, a spear-thrower, extends a hunter's arm to launch a dart with far more force than a hand-thrown spear.
evt-puebloans-early-basketry: A coiled Basketmaker-era basket, the tight spiral weave that gave the early Ancestral Puebloans their archaeological name.
evt-puebloans-first-pithouses: A reconstructed pithouse at Step House, Mesa Verde, showing the earth-roofed, sunken dwellings of the first settled villages.
evt-puebloans-rock-art-basketmaker: Newspaper Rock's crowded panel of petroglyphs, a dense record of figures and symbols pecked into desert varnish over centuries.
evt-puebloans-sandal-craft: A plaited yucca-fiber sandal from the Kayenta Ancestral Puebloans, the everyday footwear woven from desert-plant leaves and cordage.
evt-puebloans-pottery-begins: A Chacoan painted canteen, an early example of the pottery that replaced baskets as the Ancestral Puebloans' main containers.
evt-puebloans-bean-cultivation: The Three Sisters planting method, with beans climbing the corn stalk above squash, the companion system beans completed.
evt-puebloans-turkey-domestication: A North American wild turkey, the bird Ancestral Puebloans bred in pens for meat, feathers, and ritual use.
evt-puebloans-first-kivas: A round, partly sunken kiva at Bandelier, the underground ceremonial chamber that grew out of the old pithouse form.
evt-puebloans-shabikeshchee: A site plan of Shabik'eshchee Village, mapping its cluster of pithouses and an early great kiva on a mesa above Chaco.
evt-puebloans-sipapu-cosmology: The sipapu, a small round hole in a kiva floor at Mesa Verde, symbolizing the place where people emerged into this world.
evt-puebloans-black-white-pottery: A black-on-white bowl from Chaco, its geometric designs hand-painted in mineral pigment over a pale clay slip.
evt-puebloans-above-ground-masonry: Taos Pueblo's stacked, above-ground rooms, the masonry-and-adobe building tradition that succeeded the pithouse.
evt-puebloans-conflict-evidence: A stone tower at Hovenweep perched on a canyon rim, the kind of defensible site that hints at rising conflict.
evt-puebloans-pueblo-bonito-founded: The towering masonry walls of Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, the great house that began as a small arc of rooms.
evt-puebloans-great-house-architecture: Pueblo Bonito seen from the canyon wall, a multi-story great house of hundreds of rooms ringing open plazas.
evt-puebloans-fajada-butte: Fajada Butte rising above Chaco Canyon, the sandstone spire whose summit holds the Sun Dagger solar marker.
evt-puebloans-timber-transport: Wooden roof beams set into a great-house wall at Chaco, timbers hauled by hand from forests dozens of miles away.
evt-puebloans-chaco-florescence: The sprawling ruins of Pueblo Bonito, the heart of Chaco Canyon at the height of its regional power.
evt-puebloans-chetro-ketl: The long rear wall of Chetro Ketl, one of the largest great houses in Chaco Canyon.
evt-puebloans-chaco-supernova: A pictograph of a hand, crescent, and star at Chaco, long thought to record the 1054 supernova that lit the sky.
evt-puebloans-great-kivas: A great kiva at Chaco, an oversized round ceremonial chamber ringed by wall niches and far larger than a household kiva.
evt-puebloans-pueblo-bonito-expansion: Aligned doorways tunneling through Pueblo Bonito, the dense room-on-room growth of its major expansion.
evt-puebloans-outlier-communities: Great-house ruins on the Chaco landscape, the architectural template echoed by outlier communities across the region.
evt-puebloans-turquoise-workshops: Cut tiles of turquoise and red argillite from Chaco, the worked stone behind its turquoise-crafting workshops.
evt-puebloans-mesoamerican-trade: A polished Chacoan turquoise pendant, the kind of prized good that moved along trade routes reaching Mesoamerica.
evt-puebloans-chocolate-consumption: A Maya vase scene of cacao being poured, the chocolate-drinking custom whose residue turns up in Chacoan jars.
evt-puebloans-chaco-hierarchy: Pueblo Bonito from above, its planned ranks of rooms and kivas hinting at a layered Chacoan social order.
evt-puebloans-chimney-rock: The twin spires of Chimney Rock in Colorado, the high pinnacles beside which Chacoans built a remote great house.
evt-puebloans-ritual-calendar: The timbered interior of a Mesa Verde kiva, the ceremonial space that anchored the Pueblo ritual year.
evt-puebloans-petroglyphs: A spiral and animal figures pecked into a rock face at Chaco Canyon, one of many petroglyph panels along the cliffs.
evt-puebloans-aztec-ruins: The masonry ruins of Aztec Ruins, a large Chaco-style great house built on the Animas River to the north.
evt-puebloans-cliff-dwellings: A multi-story dwelling tucked into a sheltered cliff alcove in Arizona, the kind of protected setting people began building into.
evt-puebloans-cliff-palace: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, tucked beneath a sandstone overhang.
evt-puebloans-balcony-house: The steep entry ladder to Balcony House at Mesa Verde, a dwelling reachable only by climbing the cliff face.
evt-puebloans-mesa-verde-flourishes: Spruce Tree House sheltered under its alcove at Mesa Verde, one of the well-preserved cliff dwellings of the area's peak.
evt-puebloans-canyon-de-chelly: Cliff dwellings set into the red sandstone wall of Canyon de Chelly, where Ancestral Puebloans built among the alcoves.
evt-puebloans-defensive-sites: Cliff Palace recessed into its alcove at Mesa Verde, a hard-to-reach setting people increasingly chose for defense.
evt-puebloans-sand-canyon-massacre: Ruins in Canyons of the Ancients, the cliff-and-canyon country around Sand Canyon Pueblo where late violence is recorded.
evt-puebloans-kachina-origins: Carved kachina figures, the painted spirit-beings of a religious tradition that took shape in the late pueblos.
evt-puebloans-four-corners-abandonment: A map of the Four Corners region marking Mesa Verde, Chaco, and other sites the Ancestral Puebloans left behind.
evt-puebloans-rio-grande-migration: Taos Pueblo beside its creek in northern New Mexico, one of the Rio Grande communities where migrants resettled.
evt-puebloans-hopi-migration: The village of Walpi perched atop a Hopi mesa in Arizona, a defensible height where migrating families rebuilt.
evt-puebloans-dendrochronology: The growth rings of a tree cross-section, the annual bands that let researchers date Puebloan timbers to the exact year.
evt-puebloans-richard-wetherill: Cliff Palace photographed in 1891, soon after rancher Richard Wetherill came upon the ruin in Mesa Verde's cliffs.
evt-puebloans-mesa-verde-park: The walls of Sun Temple at Mesa Verde, one of the ruins protected when the area became a national park.
evt-puebloans-antiquities-act: Devils Tower, the first national monument proclaimed under the 1906 Antiquities Act used to safeguard antiquities.
evt-puebloans-kidder-classification: The ruins at Pecos, the New Mexico pueblo whose conferences gave the Pecos Classification its name.
evt-puebloans-chaco-world-heritage: An aerial view of Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, the heart of the complex now listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
evt-ashina-clan: The tamga, or clan brand, of the Ashina — the ruling lineage that gave the Türks their royal house.
evt-bumin-qaghan: A Turkic chieftain feasting in his yurt, carved on a 579 CE funerary couch from Xi'an — the steppe world Bumin ruled.
evt-byzantine-avars: The Avar Khaganate around 602, sprawled across the Carpathian basin on the Eastern Roman frontier.
evt-orkhon-heartland: The Orkhon River winding through the Mongolian steppe, the sacred heartland of the Türk khaganate.
evt-tribute-from-china: Northern Zhou in 577 — one of the rival Chinese states that bought peace from the Türks with silk.
evt-sogdian-merchants: Sogdian donors painted in a Bezeklik cave temple — the merchant diaspora that ran the Türk silk trade.
evt-bukhara-samarkand: The Afrasiab murals from Samarkand, a glimpse of the wealthy Sogdian cities the Türks now overlooked.
evt-silk-road-control: The reach of the Türk realm across the steppe, astride the overland silk routes.
evt-persian-silk-quarrel: Sogdia, whose merchants pressed the Türks to break the Persian chokehold on the silk trade.
evt-maniakh-byzantium: The First Türk Khaganate at its height — the empire whose envoy Maniakh rode all the way to Constantinople.
evt-hephthalites: The Hephthalite Empire around 500, the steppe power straddling the routes south of the Türks.
evt-khusrau-alliance: A Sasanian plate showing a crowned king — Khosrow I, the Persian ally who joined the Türks against the Hephthalites.
evt-hephthalite-destruction: A late Hephthalite coin — the last coinage of a state the Türks and Persians carved up between them.
evt-kumis-drinking: Kumis, the fermented mare's milk that fueled steppe feasts and shocked visiting envoys.
evt-east-west-split: A groom and saddled horse in a 7th-century tomb mural from Mongolia, painted as the khaganate split in two.
evt-tardu-westward: The Western Türk Khaganate, the half Tardu pushed to rule in his own right.
evt-sui-rise: The Sui dynasty in 581 — the regime that reunified China and faced the Türks as one power again.
evt-tang-founding: Emperor Gaozu of Tang, who took the throne with Türk cavalry at his back.
evt-tang-conquest-630: The Tang campaign that shattered the Eastern Türks in 630 and captured their qaghan.
evt-tang-taizong-tian-kehan: Emperor Taizong of Tang, hailed by the steppe tribes as Heavenly Qaghan.
evt-tibet-rivalry: The Tibetan Empire at its peak, the rising rival pressing on the Türk and Tang frontiers.
evt-682-revolt: The Second Türk Khaganate, the state reborn from the revolt of 682.
evt-ilterish-qaghan: The territory Ilterish Qaghan reclaimed when he raised the Türks in rebellion.
evt-kul-tigin: The carved head of Kul Tigin, recovered at his memorial complex in the Orkhon valley.
evt-bilge-kagan: An 8th-century marble statue of Bilge Qaghan from his memorial on the Orkhon.
evt-orkhon-inscriptions: The Kul Tigin stele of the Orkhon Inscriptions — the oldest known Turkic writing, carved into stone.
evt-old-turkic-script: Old Turkic runiform script, reproduced here on a modern Azerbaijani banknote that honors the steppe alphabet.
evt-bilge-warning: Bilge Qaghan's memorial stele in Mongolia, whose inscription warns the Türks against being seduced by China.
evt-734-poisoning: A Türk gold diadem of the era, the kind of treasure that adorned a qaghan in life and in the grave.
evt-uyghur-khaganate: Bögü Qaghan kneeling before a Manichean priest — the Uyghur ruler whose conversion defined the new khaganate.
evt-talas-battle: The Battle of Talas, 751 — where Tang and Abbasid armies clashed and the Karluks switched sides.
evt-khazar-future: The Khazar Khaganate north of the Caucasus, a western Türk offshoot that grew into a power of its own.
evt-bulgar-pechenegs: Pecheneg horsemen routing the Rus in a Byzantine manuscript — Turkic steppe raiders on Europe's edge.
evt-modern-turks: Where Turkic languages are spoken today, from Turkey to Siberia — the steppe legacy made permanent.
evt-tang-an-lushan: The An Lushan Rebellion that gutted the Tang and scattered Türk soldiers across the empire.
evt-early-bronze-working: A carved stone mould from Palaikastro for casting bronze double-axes, the toolkit of Crete's early metalworkers.
evt-aksum-founding: Gold coins of an early Aksumite king — the kingdom minted its own currency, a sign of the wealth that announced its arrival as a power.
evt-aksum-mani-four-empires: A rock-crystal seal carved with the prophet Mani, who ranked Aksum among the four great empires of his age.
evt-aksum-adulis-port: Excavated foundations at Adulis, the Red Sea port that funneled Aksum's trade with Rome, Arabia, and India.
evt-aksum-periplus: A map of the routes in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, the first-century sailor's guide that names Aksum and its port of Adulis.
evt-aksum-zoskales: A scale model of an Aksumite royal complex, evoking the realm Zoskales ruled when the Periplus named him.
evt-aksum-ivory-trade: Traders display elephant tusks — ivory was Aksum's signature export, shipped out through Adulis to markets across the ancient world.
evt-aksum-stelae-field: The northern stelae park at Axum, where towering carved granite obelisks marked the tombs of Aksumite kings.
evt-aksum-great-stela: The shattered blocks of the Great Stela, the largest obelisk the Aksumites ever raised — it collapsed, probably as it was being erected.
evt-aksum-stone-quarrying: Carved granite fragments from Aksum, showing the stone-working skill behind the kingdom's monumental obelisks and tombs.
evt-aksum-geez-script: A page of Ge'ez script, the alphabet Aksum developed from earlier South Arabian writing and still used by Ethiopia's church.
evt-aksum-coinage: Gold coins of King Ezana — Aksum was one of the few ancient states to strike its own gold, silver, and bronze coinage.
evt-aksum-endubis: Gold coins of King Endubis, the first Aksumite ruler to mint coinage in his own name, around 270 CE.
evt-aksum-aphilas: Coins of King Aphilas, who experimented with new denominations and the distinctive portrait styles of early Aksumite currency.
evt-aksum-tomb-brick-arches: Inside an Aksumite royal tomb, where dressed-stone passages and chambers show the engineering hidden beneath the stelae field.
evt-aksum-frumentius: An icon of Frumentius, the Syrian captive who became Aksum's first bishop and brought Christianity to the royal court.
evt-aksum-ella-amida: Coins of King Ousanas (Ella Amida), the ruler whose reign bridged Aksum's pagan past and its Christian future.
evt-aksum-ezana: The Ezana Stone, the inscribed monument of King Ezana, Aksum's most celebrated ruler and the king who made it Christian.
evt-aksum-christianity: An Ethiopian priest with hand crosses and an ancient manuscript — the living heir of the Christianity Aksum adopted in the 4th century.
evt-aksum-cross-on-coins: A late Aksumite coin stamped with a cross, marking the kingdom's shift from the old disc-and-crescent symbol to Christian imagery.
evt-aksum-cathedral: The Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Axum, Ethiopia's holiest sanctuary, on the site first consecrated in Aksumite times.
evt-aksum-ezana-stone: Ezana's trilingual inscription in Greek, Sabaean, and Ge'ez — a royal record of his campaigns and his turn to the one God.
evt-aksum-athanasius-letter: A Byzantine mosaic of Athanasius of Alexandria, the patriarch who wrote to Aksum's kings about their newly ordained bishop.
evt-aksum-kaleb: Coins of King Kaleb, who at the height of Aksumite power launched the campaign across the Red Sea into Yemen.
evt-aksum-dhu-nuwas: A 6th-century rock inscription left by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas near Najran, where he massacred the Christian community.
evt-aksum-yemen-conquest: A map of Himyar in southern Arabia, the kingdom across the Red Sea that Aksum's King Kaleb invaded and conquered.
evt-aksum-abraha: A medieval Persian painting of Abraha's war elephants — the Aksumite general who seized Yemen for himself and marched on Mecca.
evt-aksum-cosmas: A page from the Christian Topography of Cosmas Indicopleustes, the merchant-monk who described Adulis and Aksum firsthand.
evt-aksum-kaleb-abdication: The tomb attributed to King Kaleb (St. Elesbaan), who abdicated his throne and withdrew to a monastery in his final years.
evt-aksum-wa-za-eb-gebeaz: An Ethiopian icon of King Gebre Meskel, Kaleb's son, remembered for a reign of church-building and cultural flowering.
evt-aksum-nine-saints: A church mural of the Nine Saints, the foreign monks who spread monasticism and translated scripture across Aksumite Ethiopia.
evt-aksum-debre-damo: The clifftop monastery of Debre Damo, founded in Aksumite times and still reached only by climbing a rope up the sheer rock.
evt-aksum-garima-gospels: An evangelist portrait from the Garima Gospels, the illuminated Aksumite manuscripts that are among the oldest surviving Christian books.
evt-aksum-yared: A painting of Saint Yared singing before the enthroned king, the deacon who composed Ethiopia's sacred chant tradition.
evt-aksum-aksumite-liturgy: The chapel at Axum said to house the Ark of the Covenant — a focus of the Ge'ez liturgical tradition rooted in Aksumite worship.
evt-aksum-manuscript-illumination: A vivid Ethiopian church painting, heir to the manuscript-illumination tradition that took root in Aksumite monasteries.
evt-aksum-first-hijra: A medieval Islamic painting of the first Hijra, when early Muslims fleeing Mecca found refuge at the Aksumite court.
evt-aksum-dahlak-islands: A relief map of the Dahlak Archipelago off the Red Sea coast, the islands Aksum lost as its maritime power waned.
evt-aksum-kebra-nagast: An Ethiopian painting of Solomon receiving the Queen of Sheba, the royal origin story that the Kebra Nagast wove into Ethiopian legend.
evt-aksum-gudit: Toppled and weathered stelae in the fields near Axum, evoking the wreckage tradition blames on Queen Gudit's revolt.
evt-aksum-palace: The stone foundations of Dungur, the sprawling elite residence at Axum popularly known as the Queen of Sheba's palace.
evt-aksum-south-arabian-heritage: The Great Temple of Yeha, a towering Sabaean sanctuary built centuries before Aksum — the South Arabian inheritance the kingdom grew out of.
evt-aksum-rome-trade: A Roman-era trade amphora recovered near the Red Sea — the kind of vessel that carried wine and oil along Aksum's lucrative trade with the empire.
evt-aksum-najashi: The mosque at Negash, on the site of Ethiopia's oldest, honoring the Najashi — the Aksumite king who sheltered the first Muslim refugees.
evt-istemi-yabghu: A Western Türk coin struck at Tashkent around 580-610, from the western half of the empire Istemi built.
evt-otuken-mountain: The Khangai highlands of central Mongolia, the sacred Ötüken country the Türks held as the center of the world.
evt-anxi-protectorate: The Tang Empire and its Central Asian protectorates around 660, with the Anxi command planted over the old Türk lands.
evt-kucha-kashgar: The Subashi temple ruins near Kucha, remains of one of the rich Buddhist oasis-cities the Tang garrisoned.
evt-talas-precursor: The Tang Empire at its greatest extent, reaching across the old Western Türk lands deep into Central Asia.
evt-seljuk-future: The Seljuk Empire around 1092, the realm Turkic migrants carved out of the Islamic world centuries after the Türks fell.
